stances.claim: The Philippine Supreme Court has broader judicial review power than the US Supreme Court because of the second paragraph of Section 1 Article VIII -- the grave-abuse-of-discretion clause -- which allows Philippine courts to review political acts that would be non-justiciable under the US political question doctrine. This is CJP's most compact statement of Philippine judicial exceptionalism in the corpus.
stances.rhetorical_move: Philippine-judicial-exceptionalism argument: the grave-abuse-of-discretion clause as the specifically Philippine expansion of judicial review beyond the US political question limit
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing constitutional comparison

notable_anecdotes: The Eisenhower liberal duo: the introduction references Eisenhower's unintended creation of liberal judicial activists (Warren and Brennan) -- the governing US precedent for the activism-vs-restraint tension the lecture addresses.

Grave abuse of discretion definition: the full Philippine constitutional law standard -- 'capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment by reason of passion or personal hostility in a manner so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined... or any action done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence' -- is the most precise legal definition in the corpus.

Ten independence guarantees: fiscal autonomy, security of tenure, protection from removal, non-diminution of powers, administrative supervision, continuing education, freedom from congressional confirmation, bar admission control, rule-making power, and protection of constitutional rights -- the most comprehensive judicial independence checklist in the corpus.

one_paragraph_summary: Published April 29, 2008 as the outline or lecture notes for a presentation titled 'The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint,' this document by CJP is structured as topic labels with brief descriptions rather than a full speech transcript. It begins with the Eisenhower-liberal-duo framing (CJ Earl Warren and Justice William Brennan as Eisenhower's unintended activist appointees). It covers the major sources of Philippine law (constitutional, political, commercial and remedial law; civil and criminal law), the Philippine governmental structure (separation of powers), and the definition of judicial power under Section 1 Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution: (1) settling actual controversies involving legally demandable rights; (2) determining grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. The definition of grave abuse of discretion is given in full: 'Capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment by reason of passion or personal hostility in a manner so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined, or to act at all in contemplation of law. Also, any action done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence.' The outline compares the Philippine grave-abuse-of-discretion jurisdiction with the US political question doctrine. It lists ten measures guaranteeing judicial independence: fiscal autonomy; security of tenure and compensation; protection from removal; non-diminution of powers; administrative supervision over lower courts; continuing judicial education; freedom from congressional confirmation; control of bar admission; rule-making power; and protection and enforcement of constitutional rights. It closes with the ACID problems (Access, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay) and the four-Ins vision (Independence, Integrity, Industry, Intelligence) safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.
